claim: Sound location coding has been extensively studied at the central nucleus of the mammalian inferior colliculus (CNIC), supporting a population code.
source: Sound location coding has been extensively studied at the central nucleus of the mammalian inferior colliculus (CNIC), supporting a population code.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research on CNIC and population coding, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The population code for sound location has not been extensively characterized on the single-trial level with simultaneous recordings at the dorsal cortex of inferior colliculus (DCIC).
source: However, this population code has not been extensively characterized on the single-trial level with simultaneous recordings or at other anatomical regions like the dorsal cortex of inferior colliculus (DCIC), which is relevant for learning-induced experience dependent plasticity.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Large-scale recordings of DCIC populations were made from awake mice using volumetric two-photon calcium imaging with approximately 700 cells simultaneously recorded.
source: here we made in two complementary ways large-scale recordings of DCIC populations from awake mice in response to sounds delivered from 13 different frontal horizontal locations (azimuths): volumetric two-photon calcium imaging with ~700 cells simultaneously recorded at a relatively low temporal resolution
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and sample size used in the study.

claim: High-density single-unit extracellular recordings captured approximately 20 cells simultaneously at high temporal resolution.
source: high-density single-unit extracellular recordings with ~20 cells simultaneously recorded at a high temporal resolution
evidence: This describes the complementary electrophysiological recording methodology and sample size.

claim: DCIC population responses revealed substantial trial-to-trial variation (neuronal noise) that was significantly correlated across pairs of neurons (noise correlations) in the passively listening condition.
source: the recorded DCIC population responses revealed substantial trial-to-trial variation (neuronal noise) which was significantly correlated across pairs of neurons (noise correlations) in the passively listening condition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Noisy response patterns from DCIC encode sound location on a single-trial basis, reaching errors that match the discrimination ability of mice.
source: Nevertheless, decoding analysis supported that these noisy response patterns encode sound location on the single-trial basis, reaching errors that match the discrimination ability of mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from decoding analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Detected noise correlations contributed to minimize the error of the DCIC population code of sound azimuth.
source: The detected noise correlations contributed to minimize the error of the DCIC population code of sound azimuth.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis comparing decoding performance with and without noise correlations.

claim: DCIC can encode sound location in a similar format to what has been proposed for CNIC.
source: Altogether these findings point out that DCIC can encode sound location in a similar format to what has been proposed for CNIC
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the study's findings to previous work on CNIC.

claim: In vertebrates, sound localization relies on both binaural cues such as interaural level and time differences (ILD, ITD) and monaural cues including spectral notches (SN).
source: In vertebrates, sound localization relies on both binaural cues such as interaural level and time differences (ILD, ITD; Knudsen and Konishi, 1979)⁠ and monaural cues including spectral notches (SN; Kulkarni and Colburn, 1998)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sound localization cues are processed independently at brainstem nuclei in the ascending auditory pathway and integrated altogether for the first time at the inferior colliculus (IC).
source: These sound localization cues are processed independently at brainstem nuclei in the ascending auditory pathway and integrated altogether for the first time at the inferior colliculus (IC; Adams, 1979; Brunso-Bechtold et al., 1981; Gourévitch and Portfors, 2018; Grothe et al., 2010)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The IC is a crucial early relay of the ascending auditory pathway to study how a primary neural representation of auditory space is formed.
source: This makes the IC a crucial early relay of the ascending auditory pathway to study how a primary neural representation of auditory space is formed (Gourévitch and Portfors, 2018; Grothe et al., 2010)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The IC is targeted by cortico-fugal interactions involved in higher order functions concerning sound localization information like experience-dependent plasticity.
source: Furthermore, the IC is also targeted by cortico-fugal interactions involved in higher order functions concerning sound localization information like experience-dependent plasticity (Bajo et al., 2019; Bajo et al., 2010; Bajo and King, 2012)⁠
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Average responses from IC neurons were tuned to multiple sound location cues, evidencing the integration of such cues at IC.
source: Previous studies involving extracellular recordings from the mammalian IC revealed that average responses from IC neurons were tuned to multiple sound location cues, evidencing the integration of such cues at IC (Chase and Young, 2005)⁠.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from prior research with citation.

claim: The amount of sound location information carried by individual neurons throughout the auditory pathway is limited and quite variable, suggesting that the sound location information is distributed into a population code for auditory space.
source: However, the amount of sound location information carried by individual neurons throughout the auditory pathway is limited and quite variable, suggesting that the sound location information is distributed into a population code for auditory space (Clarey et al., 1995; Day and Delgutte, 2016; Groh et al., 2003; Panniello et al., 2018)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sound location in the horizontal plane (azimuth) is represented at the mammalian IC by the activity patterns of populations of neurons that display average response tuning to azimuth.
source: Fundamental work by Day and Delgutte, 2013 supports that sound location in the horizontal plane (azimuth) is represented at the mammalian IC by the activity patterns of populations of neurons that display average response tuning to azimuth, while ruling out other possibilities such as a topological code, an opposing two channel model or a population vector code (Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Georgopoulos et al., 1982)⁠.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from prior research with citations.

claim: Previous knowledge about IC population activity patterns stems from prospective patterns that were approximated by pooling non-simultaneous extracellular recordings and relied on extensive resampling.
source: Nevertheless, this knowledge stems from prospective IC population activity patterns that were approximated by pooling non-simultaneous extracellular recordings and relied on extensive resampling of the pooled recordings to increase the number of 'virtual' trials analyzed.
evidence: This statement describes limitations of prior research methods.

claim: It remains an open question whether the actual activity patterns occurring in the IC of awake animals during single-trials can encode sound location given emerging properties such as correlated neuronal noise.
source: Therefore, it remains an open question whether the actual activity patterns occurring in the IC of awake animals during single-trials can encode sound location given emerging properties such as correlated neuronal noise (Averbeck et al., 2006; Kohn et al., 2016; Sadeghi et al., 2019)⁠.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap and is supported by citations.

claim: Trial-to-trial response variability (neuronal noise) and neuronal noise correlation can have a profound impact on the neural representations of sensory information, but this can only be determined through simultaneous large-scale recordings.
source: Trial-to-trial response variability (neuronal noise) and neuronal noise correlation can have a profound impact on the neural representations of sensory information, but this can only be determined through simultaneous large-scale recordings (Averbeck et al., 2006; Kohn et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Traditional microelectrode recordings were mostly performed at a relatively deep anatomical subdivision of IC (central nucleus, CNIC), usually not targeting superficial regions (dorsal cortex, DCIC; external cortex, ECIC).
source: Finally, traditional microelectrode recordings were mostly performed at a relatively deep anatomical subdivision of IC (central nucleus, CNIC), usually not targeting superficial regions (dorsal cortex, DCIC; external cortex, ECIC; Chase and Young, 2008; Chase and Young, 2005; Day and Delgutte, 2013; Guo et al., 2016; Lesica et al., 2010; Schnupp and King, 1997)⁠.
evidence: This statement describes the focus of prior research with citations.

claim: Multichannel silicon probes and fast volumetric Ca2+ imaging enable routine simultaneous recordings from large numbers of neurons in vivo.
source: Recent technical developments, including multichannel silicon probes (Jun et al., 2017)⁠ and fast volumetric Ca2+ imaging (Prevedel et al., 2016; Stringer et al., 2019; Weisenburger et al., 2019)⁠ enable routine simultaneous recordings from large numbers of neurons in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to technical developments.

claim: The topological distribution of neurons sensitive to sound azimuth has been reported to be random at CNIC.
source: Beyond their high throughput, volumetric methods are also a promising approach to precisely interrogate the topological distribution of neurons sensitive to sound azimuth, which has been reported to be random at CNIC (Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠, but is understudied at DCIC.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The study implemented scanned temporal focusing two-photon microscopy (sTeFo 2P) to simultaneously record the activity of unprecedentedly large DCIC populations.
source: In this work, we implemented scanned temporal focusing two-photon microscopy (sTeFo 2 P; Prevedel et al., 2016)⁠, an advanced volumetric Ca2+ imaging modality, to simultaneously record the activity of unprecedentedly large DCIC populations.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: DCIC is defined as the dorsomedial IC region covering CNIC.
source: Here, we refer to DCIC as the dorsomedial IC region covering CNIC (Zhou and Shore, 2006)⁠.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation.

claim: The response patterns from mammalian DCIC populations effectively encode sound location on the single-trial basis in spite of their variability across trials.
source: Our approach produced direct evidence supporting that the response patterns from mammalian DCIC populations effectively encode sound location on the single-trial basis in spite of their variability across trials.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Substantial noise correlations were detected which can contribute to reducing the error of the population code.
source: We also detected the occurrence of substantial noise correlations which can contribute to reducing the error of this population code.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Imaging results were complemented with electrophysiological recordings with neuropixels probes, reaching conclusions that were generally aligned across imaging and electrophysiological experiments.
source: Furthermore, we complemented our imaging results with electrophysiological recordings with neuropixels probes (Jun et al., 2017)⁠, reaching conclusions that were generally aligned across imaging and electrophysiological experiments.
evidence: This describes the complementary experimental approach and consistency of findings.

claim: DCIC has a functional role in sound location coding following a similar population coding mechanism to what has been proposed for CNIC.
source: Altogether, our findings point to a functional role of DCIC in sound location coding following a similar population coding mechanism to what has been proposed for CNIC (Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings with reference to prior work.

claim: CNIC is the main ascending relay carrying sound location information from brainstem auditory nuclei to the cortex through the auditory thalamus.
source: While CNIC is the main ascending relay carrying sound location information from brainstem auditory nuclei to the cortex through the auditory thalamus (Adams, 1979; Brunso-Bechtold et al., 1981; Gourévitch and Portfors, 2018)⁠⁠
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DCIC is a higher order relay receiving profuse descending corticofugal inputs influencing auditory information processing including sound location.
source: DCIC is a higher order relay receiving profuse descending corticofugal inputs influencing auditory information processing including sound location (Bajo et al., 2019; Bajo et al., 2010; Bajo and King, 2012; Lesicko et al., 2022; Winer et al., 2002)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: AAV transduced IC neurons expressing jRGECO1a were imaged through a cranial window in awake head-fixed mice.
source: Adeno-associated viral vector (AAV) transduced IC neurons expressing jRGECO1a (Figure 1A) were imaged through a cranial window in awake head-fixed mice
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Mice passively listened to 500 ms-long broad-band noise stimuli (20–40 kHz band-passed white noise) delivered by a motorized speaker every 5 s located at one of 13 different frontal azimuth angles in a random order covering the frontal hemifield in 15° steps.
source: passively listening to 500 ms-long broad-band noise stimuli (20–40 kHz band-passed white noise) delivered by a motorized speaker every 5 s located at one of 13 different frontal azimuth angles in a random order covering the frontal hemifield in 15° steps (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulation protocol.

claim: Volumetric Ca2+ imaging (4 Hz volume rate) simultaneously sampled the activity of up to 2535 regions-of-interest (ROIs) within a 470 x 470 × 500 µm volume from the right IC unilaterally.
source: We performed volumetric Ca2+ imaging (4 Hz volume rate) simultaneously sampling the activity of up to 2535 (643±427, median ±median absolute deviation, n=12 mice) regions-of-interest (ROIs) that had a shape and size consistent with an IC neuronal soma (12–30 µm diameter, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Schofield and Beebe, 2019), within a 470 x 470 × 500 µm volume from the right IC unilaterally
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and sample characteristics.

claim: The imaged volume covered most of the dorso-ventral span of the anterior DCIC and perhaps reached the upper surface of CNIC below DCIC at more posterior locations.
source: covering most of the dorso-ventral span of the anterior DCIC (Figure 1A–C) and perhaps reaching the upper surface of CNIC below DCIC at more posterior locations (Paxinos and Franklin, 2001)⁠.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the imaged volume with citation to reference atlas.

claim: sTeFo 2P trades off spatial resolution for acquisition speed to produce volume rates compatible with the kinetics of Ca2+ sensors (voxel size: 3.7 x 3.7 × 15 µm).
source: Since sTeFo 2 P trades off spatial resolution for acquisition speed to produce volume rates compatible with the kinetics of Ca2+ sensors (voxel size: 3.7 x 3.7 × 15 µm; Prevedel et al., 2016)⁠
evidence: This describes a technical characteristic of the imaging method with citation.

claim: Fine spatial features of neurons such as dendrites or synaptic structures like spines could not be resolved in the images to unequivocally identify the segmented ROIs as individual neurons.
source: we could not resolve fine spatial features of neurons such as dendrites or synaptic structures like spines in our images to unequivocally identify the segmented ROIs as individual neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the imaging methodology.

claim: Spike probabilities were evaluated to compensate for the relatively slow decay time of the Ca2+ indicator signal and non-linearities in the summation of Ca2+ events.
source: To compensate for the relatively slow decay time of the Ca2+ indicator signal and non-linearities in the summation of Ca2+ events, we evaluated the spike probabilities associated to the neuronal Ca2+ signals (Deneux et al., 2016; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach with citation.

claim: The spike probability estimation does not involve predicting precise spike timings.
source: The spike probability estimation does not involve predicting precise spike timings (Deneux et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2021; Pachitariu et al., 2018; Rupprecht et al., 2021; Vanwalleghem et al., 2020)⁠.
evidence: This clarifies the nature of the spike probability estimation with citations.

claim: Spike probabilities were treated as a measure proportional to the spike count evaluated within the time interval set by the volumetric imaging rate (4 Hz).
source: Hence, we do not make any observation or interpretation of spike probabilities in relation to the fine temporal structure of neuronal spiking. Instead, we treated the spike probabilities as a measure proportional to the spike count evaluated within the time interval set by our volumetric imaging rate (4 Hz).
evidence: This describes how spike probabilities were interpreted in the analysis.

claim: The main carrier of sound location information is IC neuron firing rate.
source: Taking into account that the main carrier of sound location information is IC neuron firing rate (Chase and Young, 2008)⁠
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Evoked DCIC population responses were defined as the total (summed) spike probability of each imaged unit during the sound stimulation epoch (500ms).
source: we defined the evoked DCIC population responses as the total (summed) spike probability of each imaged unit during the sound stimulation epoch (500ms).
evidence: This describes how responses were quantified in the analysis.

claim: DCIC populations simultaneously imaged from passively listening awake mice displayed spontaneous activity that was not time-locked to the stimulation (on-going activity) and sound-evoked response patterns that varied markedly across trials.
source: The DCIC populations simultaneously imaged from passively listening awake mice displayed spontaneous activity that was not time-locked to the stimulation (on-going activity) and sound-evoked response patterns that varied markedly across trials, as did the overall, average response of the complete imaged population (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the experimental data.

claim: The overall average population activity shows significant correlation to facial movements, specifically of the snout region.
source: By monitoring face movements videographically, we observed that the overall average population activity shows significant correlation to facial movements, specifically of the snout region (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A—C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of face movement data.

claim: The correlation between the recorded activity from the individual units imaged and face movements was generally low with narrow distributions centered at 0.
source: On the other hand, the correlation between the recorded activity from the individual units imaged and face movements was generally low with narrow distributions centered at 0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), pointing out that correlation to face movement is more evident at the population level.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of face movement data.

claim: DCIC population activity was recorded electrophysiologically through single-unit recordings with neuropixels probes in passively listening mice stimulated with 200 ms-long broad-band noise stimuli (15–50 kHz band-passed white noise) delivered by a motorized speaker every 3 s from 13 different frontal azimuth angles in a random order covering the frontal hemifield in 15° steps.
source: we recorded DCIC population activity electrophysiologically through single-unit recordings with neuropixels probes in passively listening mice stimulated with 200 ms-long broad-band noise stimuli (15–50 kHz band-passed white noise) delivered by a motorized speaker every 3 s from 13 different frontal azimuth angles in a random order covering the frontal hemifield in 15° steps (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This describes the electrophysiological experimental methodology.

claim: The higher time resolution from the electrophysiological approach (30 kHz acquisition rate) allowed delivery of more frequent trials with shorter stimuli to effectively collect more trials.
source: The higher time resolution from the electrophysiological approach (30 kHz acquisition rate) allowed us to deliver more frequent trials with shorter stimuli to effectively collect more trials following the same head fixation paradigm as the one used for imaging (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the electrophysiological protocol design.

claim: The electrophysiology setup produced lower background noise sound pressure level (SPL, 35.96 dB R.M.S.) in comparison to the sTeFo scope (44.83 dB R.M.S.).
source: The electrophysiology setup also produced lower background noise sound pressure level (SPL, 35.96 dB R.M.S.) in comparison to the sTeFo scope (44.83 dB R.M.S.)
evidence: This describes a technical difference between the two experimental setups.

claim: Up to 43 spike sorted and manually curated DCIC single-units were simultaneously recorded (21±9, median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice).
source: We simultaneously recorded up to 43 (21±9, median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice) spike sorted and manually curated DCIC single-units (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C—E).
evidence: This describes the sample size from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Sound evoked responses from electrophysiologically recorded single-units were defined as the spike count observed during sound stimulus presentation.
source: We defined sound evoked responses from electrophysiologically recorded single-units as the spike count observed during sound stimulus presentation (Chase and Young, 2008; Day and Delgutte, 2016; Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠.
evidence: This describes how responses were quantified with citations to prior methods.

claim: Recording channels from the probe were determined to be located within DCIC both histologically with respect to the reference atlas and functionally by analyzing the arrangement of sound frequency sensitive units along the shank of the probe.
source: We determined which recording channels from the probe were located within DCIC both histologically with respect to the reference atlas (Paxinos and Franklin, 2001;⁠ Figure 1F) and functionally by analyzing the arrangement of sound frequency sensitive units along the shank of the probe.
evidence: This describes the method for determining anatomical location of recordings.

claim: Sound frequency sensitive single-units were detected as units that displayed significant response dependency to sound frequency (pure tone stimuli) through χ2 tests.
source: We detected sound frequency sensitive single-units as units that displayed significant response dependency to sound frequency (pure tone stimuli) through χ2 tests.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for identifying frequency-sensitive units.

claim: The detected frequency dependent single-units displayed Gaussian tuning with clear peak best frequencies.
source: The detected frequency dependent single-units displayed Gaussian tuning with clear peak best frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of frequency tuning data.

claim: The observed relationship between frequency-dependent DCIC unit best frequency and recording depth was not tonotopically arranged like in CNIC, which is consistent with DCIC location.
source: The observed relationship between frequency-dependent DCIC unit best frequency and recording depth was not tonotopically arranged like in CNIC, which is consistent with DCIC location (Barnstedt et al., 2015; Wong and Borst, 2019;⁠ Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of tonotopic organization with citations to prior work.

claim: The simultaneous, electrophysiologically recorded DCIC population activity from awake passively listening mice displayed spontaneous on-going activity and sound-evoked response patterns that varied markedly across trials.
source: The simultaneous, electrophysiologically recorded DCIC population activity from awake passively listening mice also displayed spontaneous on-going activity, which reflected in the overall average response of the complete recorded population, and sound-evoked response patterns that varied markedly across trials (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the electrophysiological data.

claim: When decoding all simultaneously recorded units, the observed classifier output was not significantly better than the chance level distribution.
source: When decoding all simultaneously recorded units, the observed classifier output was not significantly better (shifted towards smaller prediction errors) than the chance level distribution (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis of the complete population.

claim: The classifier failed to decode complete DCIC population responses recorded with neuropixels probes.
source: The classifier also failed to decode complete DCIC population responses recorded with neuropixels probes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The classification failure could be due to overfitting rather than to a lack of azimuth information in the dataset.
source: Given the high dimensionality of our datasets (number of simultaneously recorded units) and the relatively low number of azimuth presentations collected (10–20 repetitions of each), we reasoned that the classification failure could be due to overfitting rather than to a lack of azimuth information in the dataset.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of classification failure based on dataset characteristics.

claim: Decoding based on subsets of first principal components (PCs) produced absolute cross-validated single-trial prediction error distributions significantly better than the chance level distribution for both imaging and electrophysiological datasets.
source: For both our imaging and electrophysiological datasets, we observed that decoding based on subsets of first principal components (PCs) produced absolute cross-validated single-trial prediction error distributions significantly better than the chance level distribution (Figure 2D and E, Figure 3B–D)
evidence: This is a primary finding from decoding analysis after dimensionality reduction.

claim: Using larger numbers of PCs for model fitting and decoding decreased the performance.
source: and that using larger numbers of PCs for model fitting and decoding decreased the performance (Figure 2D and E, Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis showing overfitting with more PCs.

claim: DCIC population responses carry stimulus azimuth information which can be effectively decoded on a single-trial basis.
source: Altogether, these results support that DCIC population responses indeed carry stimulus azimuth information which can be effectively decoded on a single-trial basis
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis results.

claim: The failure of decoding from the full population was merely due to overfitting.
source: and that the failure of decoding from the full population was merely due to overfitting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing decoding performance with different numbers of features.

claim: Imaged DCIC units generally showed a relatively low nS/N during sound stimulations (<1).
source: Imaged DCIC units generally showed a relatively low nS/N during sound stimulations (<1, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of signal-to-noise ratios in the imaging data.

claim: The nS/N during sound stimulation was significantly larger than the one registered in the absence of sound stimulation (on-going activity), indicating that sound responses across the sampled units were often noisy.
source: Nevertheless, this nS/N was significantly larger than the one registered in the absence of sound stimulation (on-going activity from the periods between sound stimuli, Figures 1D and 4A), indicating that sound responses across the sampled units were often noisy.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing signal-to-noise ratios under different conditions.

claim: The broad distribution of nS/N suggested that a sparse population of neurons responded more robustly.
source: However, the broad distribution of nS/N also suggested that a sparse population of neurons responded more robustly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distribution of signal-to-noise ratios.

claim: Units with significant azimuth tuning represented only 8 ± 3% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=12 mice) of the DCIC units simultaneously-imaged in one session.
source: The units with significant azimuth tuning represented only 8 ± 3% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=12 mice) of the DCIC units simultaneously-imaged in one session (mouse; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of azimuth tuning.

claim: The percentage of units with significant azimuth tuning is not significantly different from the false positive detection rate of the ANOVA tests (α=0.05).
source: This is not significantly different from the false positive detection rate of our ANOVA tests (α=0.05, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing observed tuning to expected false positive rate.

claim: The large trial-to-trial variability in the imaged DCIC responses made it difficult to detect response specificity based on differences in median activity.
source: Given that a large number of trials showed no response at all in many units, it is possible that the large trial-to-trial variability in the imaged DCIC responses made it difficult to detect response specificity based on differences in median activity.
evidence: This is an inference about why median-based tuning detection was ineffective.

claim: Units with significant response dependency to stimulus azimuth (p<0.05) represented 32 ± 6% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=12 mice) of the units simultaneously imaged in one session.
source: The units with significant response dependency to stimulus azimuth (p<0.05) represented 32 ± 6% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=12 mice) of the units simultaneously imaged in one session (mouse, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from χ2 tests for response dependency.

claim: Top ranked units typically did not respond in many trials; nevertheless, their evoked responses showed a tendency to be more selective towards contralateral or central stimulus azimuths.
source: Even the top ranked units typically did not respond in many trials; nevertheless, their evoked responses showed a tendency to be more selective towards contralateral or central stimulus azimuths (Figure 4D left inset).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of top ranked unit responses.

claim: The nS/N of top ranked units was significantly larger than the one registered in the absence of sound stimulation, but these units did not display a major improvement in nS/N with respect to the complete population of imaged units.
source: The nS/N of top ranked units was also significantly larger than the one registered in the absence of sound stimulation, but these units did not display a major improvement in nS/N with respect to the complete population of imaged units, indicating that despite their response dependency to stimulus azimuth their responses are also noisy (Figure 4A and D right inset).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing signal-to-noise ratios of top ranked units.

claim: The single-trial response patterns of at least the 7 top ranked units produced stimulus azimuth prediction errors that were significantly smaller than chance level (p=6 x 10–4, Kolmogorov-Smirnov with Sidak) using Bayes classification.
source: We found that the single-trial response patterns of at least the 7 top ranked units produced stimulus azimuth prediction errors that were significantly smaller than chance level (p=6 x 10–4, Kolmogorov-Smirnov with Sidak) using Bayes classification (naive approximation, for computation efficiency; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from decoding analysis of top ranked units.

claim: Increasing the number of top ranked units decoded did not bring major improvements in decoder performance (plateau), up to a point where performance dropped, due to classifier overfitting.
source: Increasing the number of top ranked units decoded did not bring major improvements in decoder performance (plateau), up to a point where performance dropped, due to classifier overfitting likely caused by the relatively small number of collected trials per class (Figure 4G, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis showing overfitting with more units.

claim: The single-trial response patterns from subsamples of at least the 7 top ranked units produced median decoding errors that coincidentally matched the reported azimuth discrimination ability of mice (minimum audible angle = 31°).
source: If we consider the median of the prediction error distribution as an overall measure of decoding performance, the single-trial response patterns from subsamples of at least the 7 top ranked units produced median decoding errors that coincidentally matched the reported azimuth discrimination ability of mice (Figure 4G, minimum audible angle = 31°; Lauer et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis compared to behavioral data from prior research.

claim: The top ranked units (~32% from the complete DCIC populations imaged) are scattered across the imaged volumes following the same distributions across the anatomical axes of the complete imaged populations.
source: By comparing the positions of top ranked units to those of the complete samples of simultaneously imaged units across mice, we observed that the top ranked units (~32% from the complete DCIC populations imaged) are scattered across the imaged volumes following the same distributions across the anatomical axes of the complete imaged populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from spatial analysis of top ranked unit positions.

claim: The subpopulations of top ranked DCIC units associated with the population code of sound azimuth scatter across the DCIC without following a specific spatial pattern.
source: This observation suggests that the subpopulations of top ranked DCIC units associated with the population code of sound azimuth scatter across the DCIC without following a specific spatial pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial distribution analysis.

claim: Top ranked units detected in neuropixels datasets displayed response selectivity towards contralateral and central azimuths and did not respond in many trials.
source: Top ranked units detected in our neuropixels datasets also displayed response selectivity towards contralateral and central azimuths and did not respond in many trials (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The nS/N of the DCIC single-units recorded with neuropixels was significantly larger than the one registered without sound stimulation, with a distribution tailing above 1.
source: The nS/N of the DCIC single-units recorded with neuropixels was again significantly larger than the one registered without sound stimulation, with a distribution tailing above 1.
evidence: This is a finding from signal-to-noise analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Top ranked units from neuropixels displayed a further shift towards higher nS/N with respect to the complete population of neuropixels recorded DCIC single-units, but the medians of these nS/N distributions was below 1, supporting that DCIC single-unit responses are noisy.
source: Top ranked units displayed a further shift towards higher nS/N with respect to the complete population of neuropixels recorded DCIC single-units. Still the medians of these nS/N distributions was below 1, supporting that DCIC single-unit responses are noisy (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from signal-to-noise analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Top ranked units detected with neuropixels recordings represented 40 ± 2% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice) of the units simultaneously recorded in an experiment.
source: Top ranked units detected with neuropixels recordings represented 40 ± 2% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice) of the units simultaneously recorded in an experiment (mouse, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The nS/N distributions of neuropixels recorded DCIC single-units in response to pure tone stimuli were similar to those observed for broadband stimulus azimuth.
source: Interestingly, the nS/N distributions of neuropixels recorded DCIC single-units in response to pure tone stimuli were similar to those observed for broadband stimulus azimuth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, Figure 5C)
evidence: This is a finding from comparing signal-to-noise ratios across stimulus types.

claim: The observed nS/N levels in imaging and electrophysiological recordings might be a property of the DCIC network which is noisy independently of the stimulus presented, at least in the passively listening condition.
source: suggesting that the observed nS/N levels in our imaging and electrophysiological recordings might be a property of the DCIC network (and not due to the recording method's sensitivity) which is noisy independently of the stimulus presented, at least in the passively listening condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing signal-to-noise ratios across methods and stimuli.

claim: The percentage of sound frequency dependent units was 42 ± 15% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice).
source: The percentage of sound frequency dependent units was 42 ± 15% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of frequency tuning in electrophysiological data.

claim: 19 ± 6% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice) of DCIC single-units from neuropixels recordings displayed significant response dependency to both broadband stimulus azimuth and pure tone stimulus frequency.
source: Out of the DCIC single-units from our neuropixels recordings, 19 ± 6% (median ±median absolute deviation, n=4 mice, Figure 5D) displayed significant response dependency to both broadband stimulus azimuth and pure tone stimulus frequency
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of dual sensitivity in electrophysiological data.

claim: Not all DCIC azimuth-dependent units are sensitive to sound frequency and vice versa.
source: pointing out that not all DCIC azimuth-dependent units are sensitive to sound frequency and vice versa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of dual sensitivity.

claim: The correlation between best frequency and azimuth sensitivity of units sensitive to both was low (R=0.03, 17 single-units from 4 mice).
source: To explore a possible relationship between the best frequency and azimuth sensitivity of these units in the context of the duplex theory (Rayleigh, 1907)⁠, we evaluated the correlation between their best frequency and the significance level of their response dependency to azimuth (-log(p value) of the χ2 test). This correlation was low (R=0.03, 17 single-units from 4 mice)
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of frequency and azimuth sensitivity.

claim: The clear majority of units sensitive to both frequency and azimuth had best frequencies above ~10 kHz, where the main sound location cues used by mice are carried.
source: but we could observe that the clear majority of these units had best frequencies above ~10 kHz, where the main sound location cues used by mice are carried (Lauer et al., 2011;⁠ Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of best frequencies with citation to prior work on mouse sound localization cues.

claim: The 4 top ranked units are the smallest subsample necessary to produce a significant decoding performance that coincidentally matches the discrimination ability of mice (31°) in neuropixels recordings.
source: Decoding analysis (Figure 4F) of the population response patterns from azimuth dependent top ranked units simultaneously recorded with neuropixels probes showed that the 4 top ranked units are the smallest subsample necessary to produce a significant decoding performance that coincidentally matches the discrimination ability of mice (31° (Lauer et al., 2011;⁠ Figure 5F and G)).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis of electrophysiological data with citation to behavioral data.

claim: Even though noisy DCIC single-units can encode sound location individually with low performance, a population code consisting of the simultaneous response patterns from small subsets of top ranked units occurs at DCIC, achieving more effective encoding errors.
source: Altogether, the close resemblance of the results obtained through volumetric imaging and electrophysiologically with neuropixels support that, even though noisy DCIC single-units can encode sound location individually with low performance (Figure 5F and G, first top ranked unit), a population code consisting of the simultaneous response patterns from small subsets of top ranked units occurs at DCIC, achieving more effective encoding errors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing individual and population decoding performance across methods.

claim: Noise correlations have been previously reported to occur at mammalian IC populations and can influence the accuracy of the DCIC population code for sound azimuth.
source: We next investigated the occurrence of correlated variation in the trial-to-trial responses to each stimulus azimuth from pairs of simultaneously imaged or electrophysiologically recorded top ranked units as the occurrence of such neuronal noise correlations, which have been previously reported to occur at mammalian IC populations (Sadeghi et al., 2019), can influence the accuracy of the DCIC population code for sound azimuth (Averbeck et al., 2006; Kohn et al., 2016;⁠ Figure 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on noise correlations.

claim: Using cross-validated hierarchical clustering of the simultaneously imaged or neuropixels recorded top ranked units based on noise correlation, no clear groups (clusters, subpopulations) of highly noise correlated units were observed across the trial repetitions from each stimulus azimuth.
source: Using cross-validated hierarchical clustering of the simultaneously imaged or neuropixels recorded top ranked units based on noise correlation, we observed no clear groups (clusters, subpopulations) of highly noise correlated units across the trial repetitions from each stimulus azimuth (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from clustering analysis of noise correlations.

claim: The pairwise noise correlation coefficients observed across datasets (mice) showed a distribution that was significantly shifted towards positive values with respect to chance level.
source: However, the pairwise noise correlation coefficients observed across datasets (mice) showed a distribution that was significantly shifted towards positive values with respect to chance level, calculated from the same datasets subjected to randomization of each unit's responses across trial repetitions for each stimulus azimuth (decorrelated, Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from noise correlation analysis.

claim: The shift towards positive noise correlations was much smaller for ipsilateral and central azimuths in neuropixels data.
source: Nevertheless, this shift was much smaller for ipsilateral and central azimuths in our neuropixels data (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from noise correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Pairs of the DCIC top ranked units associated with the population code for sound azimuth display positive noise correlations with a likelihood that is higher than chance.
source: Altogether these observations suggest that pairs of the DCIC top ranked units associated with the population code for sound azimuth display positive noise correlations with a likelihood that is higher than chance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the noise correlation analysis.

claim: The modeled decorrelated datasets produced stimulus azimuth prediction error distributions that were significantly shifted towards higher decoding errors.
source: Using this classifier, we observed that the modeled decorrelated datasets produced stimulus azimuth prediction error distributions that were significantly shifted towards higher decoding errors (Figure 6B and C)
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis comparing data with and without noise correlations.

claim: In imaging datasets, the modeled decorrelated datasets were not significantly different from chance level.
source: and, in our imaging datasets, were not significantly different from chance level (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis of decorrelated imaging data.

claim: The detected noise correlations in simultaneously acquired datasets can help reduce the error of the IC population code for sound azimuth.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the detected noise correlations in our simultaneously acquired datasets can help reduce the error of the IC population code for sound azimuth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing decoding performance with and without noise correlations.

claim: sTeFo-2P effectively achieved high throughput sampling across large imaging depths in a highly light-scattering tissue such as the mouse IC.
source: We show that sTeFo-2P effectively achieved high throughput sampling across large imaging depths in a highly light-scattering tissue such as the mouse IC (Figure 1), showcasing the capability of sTeFo-2P for interrogating neuronal population activity over large volumes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the technical capabilities demonstrated in the study.

claim: Large-scale volumetric imaging has a low temporal resolution, reaching sampling rates of 4 volumes per second.
source: In particular, large-scale volumetric imaging has a low temporal resolution, reaching sampling rates of 4 volumes per second
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the imaging method.

claim: The low temporal resolution effectively produces a low-pass filtering of neuronal activity, misrepresenting peak responses.
source: The low temporal resolution effectively produces a low-pass filtering of neuronal activity, misrepresenting peak responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of low temporal resolution on data quality.

claim: Indirectly inferring neuronal spiking responses from Ca2+ sensor signals can cause further information loss.
source: Furthermore, indirectly inferring neuronal spiking responses from Ca2+ sensor signals can cause further information loss.
evidence: This describes a limitation of calcium imaging methodology.

claim: The main observations drawn from sTeFo 2P imaged population response patterns could be validated via single-unit recordings with neuropixels probes.
source: Nevertheless, the main observations drawn from sTeFo 2 P imaged population response patterns could be validated via single-unit recordings with new generation multichannel silicon probes (neuropixels), which have excellent temporal resolution but markedly lower throughput.
evidence: This describes the validation of imaging findings with electrophysiology.

claim: The sTeFo imaging datasets still carried sufficient information about stimulus azimuth.
source: This supports that the sTeFo imaging datasets still carried sufficient information about stimulus azimuth (Figures 2 and 4)
evidence: This is a conclusion about the information content of imaging data.

claim: The single-trial response patterns from subsets of neurons with response dependency to stimulus azimuth (top ranked units) constitute a population code for sound azimuth at the DCIC of awake, passively listening mice.
source: The imaged or electrophysiologically recorded population activity datasets here described support with simultaneous recordings that the single-trial response patterns from subsets of neurons with response dependency to stimulus azimuth (top ranked units) constitute a population code for sound azimuth at the DCIC of awake, passively listening mice (Figures 4–5).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: This finding complements previous studies analyzing pooled, non-simultaneous extracellular recordings from the CNIC of passively listening animals.
source: This finding complements previous studies analyzing pooled, non-simultaneous extracellular recordings from the CNIC of passively listening animals (Day et al., 2012; Day and Delgutte, 2016; Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠
evidence: This statement relates the current findings to prior research with citations.

claim: Sound location coding occurs at DCIC on the single-trial basis, and this follows a comparable mechanism to the characterized population code at CNIC.
source: Concretely, we show that sound location coding does indeed occur at DCIC on the single-trial basis, and that this follows a comparable mechanism to the characterized population code at CNIC (Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study with citation to prior work.

claim: It remains to be determined if the DCIC network is physiologically capable of Bayesian decoding computations.
source: However, it remains to be determined if indeed the DCIC network is physiologically capable of Bayesian decoding computations.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction for research.

claim: The small number of DCIC top ranked units necessary to effectively decode stimulus azimuth suggests that sound azimuth information is redundantly distributed across DCIC top ranked units.
source: Interestingly, the small number of DCIC top ranked units necessary to effectively decode stimulus azimuth suggests that sound azimuth information is redundantly distributed across DCIC top ranked units
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoding results.

claim: Mechanisms beyond coding efficiency could be relevant for this population code.
source: which points out that mechanisms beyond coding efficiency could be relevant for this population code.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of redundancy.

claim: A relationship between decoding error and psychophysical performance remains to be determined.
source: While the decoding error observed from our DCIC datasets obtained in passively listening, untrained mice coincidentally matches the discrimination ability of highly trained, motivated mice (Lauer et al., 2011), a relationship between decoding error and psychophysical performance remains to be determined.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction for research.

claim: A primary sensory representation should theoretically be even more precise than the behavioral performance as reported in the visual system.
source: Interestingly, a primary sensory representations should theoretically be even more precise than the behavioral performance as reported in the visual system (Stringer et al., 2021)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research in another sensory system.

claim: The population code of sound azimuth at DCIC is likely not a primary representation, as DCIC is reported to be involved in higher order functions including experience dependent plasticity, is influenced by auditory cortex and is associated to non-auditory processes.
source: One possible explanation could be that the population code of sound azimuth at DCIC is likely not a primary representation, as DCIC is reported to be involved in higher order functions including experience dependent plasticity, is influenced by auditory cortex (Bajo et al., 2019; Bajo et al., 2010; Bajo and King, 2012)⁠ and is associated to non-auditory processes (Gruters and Groh, 2012; Wong and Borst, 2019)⁠.
evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of DCIC representation supported by citations.

claim: A correlation was observed between the recorded DCIC population activity and snout movements, suggesting that non-auditory processes are likely influencing the recorded responses.
source: In this respect, we observed a correlation between the recorded DCIC population activity and snout movements, suggesting that non-auditory processes are likely influencing the recorded responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from face movement analysis with an inference about non-auditory influences.

claim: Unilateral subpopulations of top ranked DCIC units carry enough information to generate a representation of the complete frontal hemifield that is accurate enough to match the discrimination ability of mice.
source: Our observations support this notion, showing that unilateral subpopulations of top ranked DCIC units carry enough information to generate a representation of the complete frontal hemifield that is accurate enough to match the discrimination ability of mice (Lauer et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings with citation to behavioral data.

claim: The jRGECO1a-labeled neurons imaged could project contralaterally, suggesting that the imaged DCIC populations would be involved in commissural interactions.
source: In this respect, we observed that the jRGECO1a-labeled neurons we imaged could project contralaterally (Figure 1A, inset), suggesting that the imaged DCIC populations would be involved in commissural interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis with an inference about functional connectivity.

claim: The actual accuracy of the DCIC population code for sound azimuth, on the single-trial basis, might only be reached if bilateral DCIC recordings were considered.
source: Thus, we cannot rule out that the actual accuracy of the DCIC population code for sound azimuth, on the single-trial basis, would only be reached if we considered bilateral DCIC recordings.
evidence: This is a speculation about a limitation of the unilateral recording approach.

claim: Both imaging and neuropixels datasets show that the responses from DCIC neurons are noisy, independently of the recording methodology or stimulus.
source: Both our imaging and neuropixels datasets show that the responses from DCIC neurons are noisy, independently of the recording methodology or stimulus (Figures 4 and 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing signal-to-noise ratios across methods and stimuli.

claim: Neuronal noise is often positively correlated across simultaneously recorded pairs of top ranked units, which are involved in the population code of sound azimuth.
source: and that this neuronal noise is often positively correlated across simultaneously recorded pairs of top ranked units, which are involved in the population code of sound azimuth (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding from noise correlation analysis.

claim: Noise correlations have been reported to occur at the mammalian CNIC and have a role in sound categorization.
source: Noise correlations have been reported to occur at the mammalian CNIC and have a role in sound categorization (Sadeghi et al., 2019)⁠
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The influence of noise correlations on the population code for sound location remained unexplored in prior studies.
source: however their influence on the population code for sound location remained unexplored (Day et al., 2012; Day and Delgutte, 2016; Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap with citations to prior work.

claim: Response sensitivity to azimuth might not be the only feature of IC neurons carrying information about stimulus azimuth, but noise correlations across the population responses could also be a relevant factor.
source: Thus, our data supports that response sensitivity to azimuth might not be the only feature of IC neurons carrying information about stimulus azimuth, as considered in previous studies (Chase and Young, 2008; Chase and Young, 2005; Day et al., 2012; Day and Delgutte, 2016; Day and Delgutte, 2013)⁠, but noise correlations across the population responses could also be a relevant factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings with citations to prior work.

claim: This implication might extend to other brain regions relevant for sound location coding or perhaps also to different sensory modalities.
source: This implication might extend to other brain regions relevant for sound location coding or perhaps also to different sensory modalities.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The study adopted the IC segmentation boundaries and labels from the Franklin-Paxinos atlas.
source: Here, we adopted the IC segmentation boundaries and labels from the Franklin-Paxinos atlas, due to the extensive previous research employing it and the fact that we followed a compatible tissue preparation procedure for determining the anatomical location of our imaged volumes and electrode tracts (PFA fixed tissue slices).
evidence: This describes the methodological choice for anatomical reference.

claim: DCIC top ranked units scatter across the imaged volume with no specificity in their location across the anatomical axes.
source: Taking this into consideration, we report that DCIC top ranked units scatter across the imaged volume with no specificity in their location across the anatomical axes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from spatial analysis of top ranked unit positions.

claim: In vivo imaging studies report that the mouse dorsal IC processes sound frequency information topographically (tonotopy), showing a distinct tonotopic arrangement of neurons across the rostromedial-caudolateral and dorso-ventral axes.
source: Interestingly, in vivo imaging studies report that the mouse dorsal IC processes sound frequency information topographically (tonotopy), showing a distinct tonotopic arrangement of neurons across the rostromedial-caudolateral and dorso-ventral axes (Barnstedt et al., 2015; Wong and Borst, 2019)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior imaging studies.

claim: Not all DCIC azimuth-sensitive units show pure tone sound frequency sensitivity, whereas a fraction of units showing both azimuth and sound frequency sensitivity displayed selectivity for high sound frequencies >10 kHz.
source: Nevertheless, we observed that not all DCIC azimuth-sensitive units show pure tone sound frequency sensitivity, whereas a fraction of units showing both azimuth and sound frequency sensitivity displayed selectivity for high sound frequencies >10 kHz
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of dual sensitivity in electrophysiological data.

claim: Simultaneous recordings from passively listening mice directly support that population response patterns from a subset of DCIC noisy neurons effectively encode sound location on the single-trial basis with an error that matches the discrimination ability of trained mice.
source: In conclusion, our simultaneous recordings from passively listening mice directly support that population response patterns from a subset of DCIC noisy neurons effectively encode sound location on the single-trial basis with an error that matches the discrimination ability of trained mice (Lauer et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion of the study with citation to behavioral data.

claim: Azimuth information is redundantly distributed across the subset of DCIC azimuth-sensitive units (top ranked units), which rely not only on response dependency to sound location but also on noise-correlations to accurately encode this information and are randomly scattered across DCIC.
source: Specifically, we report that azimuth information is redundantly distributed across the subset of DCIC azimuth-sensitive units (top ranked units), which rely not only on response dependency to sound location but also on noise-correlations to accurately encode this information and are randomly scattered across DCIC.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: An important open question remains about the behavioral relevance of this code and the noise correlations.
source: An important open question remains about the behavioral relevance of this code and the noise correlations.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction for research.

claim: TeFo-based methods have been shown to be more resilient to highly scattering (optically opaque) tissues such as the IC.
source: Moreover, TeFo-based methods have been shown to be more resilient to highly scattering (optically opaque) tissues such as the IC (Dana and Shoham, 2012)⁠.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior technical work.
